claim: The FCC authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million Starmind orbital data center satellites.

support.quote: Authority for radiofrequency communications for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking, & command (TT&C) for a constellation of 1,000,000 NGSO satellites to operate as data centers in space.

claim: The Space Bureau's November 25, 2026 order grants backup spectrum between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, sets milestones through 2040, and defers high-altitude disposal waivers.

support.quote: Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.

SpaceX must launch the remaining space stations necessary to complete its authorized constellation, place them in their assigned orbits, and operate each in accordance with this authorization no later than November 25, 2040.

Because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements, SpaceX’s waiver request is deferred.

claim: The FCC Space Bureau granted SpaceX conditional authority on November 25, 2026 for up to 1,000,000 non-geostationary orbital data center satellites under Starmind.

support.quote: Adopted: November 25, 2026 By the Chief, Space Bureau: Released: November 25, 2026
Authority for radiofrequency communications for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking, & command (TT&C) for a constellation of 1,000,000 NGSO satellites to operate as data centers in space.

claim: The FCC's November 25, 2026 release called the order the first U.S. authorization for a constellation of data centers in space, and Chairman Brendan Carr said it opens a bold new frontier.

support.quote: Today, the Federal Communications Commission granted the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.
This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.

claim: Elon Musk wrote on X on November 25, 2026 that Starmind will be a great asset to America and the world, and SpaceX shares rose 1.3% to $127.44.

support.quote: “Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world,” Musk wrote.
SpaceX shares rose 1.3% on Wednesday to $127.44.

claim: SpaceX acquired xAI Corp. shortly after filing for Starmind and featured orbital data centers in its June 2026 IPO investor pitch.

support.quote: SpaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June.

claim: Rival efforts include Blue Origin's March 2026 filing for up to 51,600 Project Sunrise satellites, Starcloud's $250 million August 2026 round, and Google's Project Suncatcher prototype satellite launched in October 2026.

support.quote: Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.
Google is testing that with Project Suncatcher, a prototype satellite that launched on a SpaceX rocket in October.

support.quote: ICFS File No. SAT-LOA-20260108-00016 Call Sign: S00798
orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.

support.quote: The System will operate at altitudes ranging from 500 km to 2,000 km and in 30 degree and sun-synchronous orbit inclinations within orbital shells spanning up to 50 km each.
requested use of the 18.3-19.3 GHz and 28.6-29.1 GHz frequency bands outside of a processing round.

claim: A U.S. Table waiver permits unprotected, non-interference backup TT&C in 18.8-19.3 GHz (space-to-Earth) and 28.6-29.1 GHz (Earth-to-space).

support.quote: waiver of the U.S. Table of Frequency Allocations, 47 CFR § 2.106(a) (U.S. Table), for SpaceX’s TT&C operations only in the 18.8-19.3 GHz (space-to-Earth) and 28.6-29.1 GHz (Earth-to-space) bands on an unprotected and non-interference basis.

claim: SpaceX must coordinate with federal national-security and safety-of-life agencies before using 18.8-19.3 GHz and immediately cease operations causing harmful interference.

support.quote: SpaceX must complete coordination with potentially affected Federal Agencies and Services engaged in national security or safety-of-life service
SpaceX must immediately cease the operations causing the harmful interference until the issue is resolved

claim: Each satellite spans 70 to 75 meters (230 to 246 feet) with radiation-hardened compute modules, a 250-kilowatt peak solar array, and a 110-square-meter (1,184-square-foot) liquid-cooled radiator array.

support.quote: Each satellite, spanning 230 to 246 feet (70 to 75 m) when deployed, houses a central rack of radiation-hardened compute modules flanked by two sets of panels.

A smaller 1,184-square-foot (110 m²) array circulates liquid through double-sided radiators angled edge-on to the Sun to vent heat into deep space. A larger solar array generates up to 250 kW of peak electrical power.

claim: Nvidia said in August 2026 SpaceX plans to adapt its Vera Rubin system for first-generation satellites, and SpaceX says its Bastrop, Texas factory could produce satellites by late 2027.

support.quote: In August (pre-Jensen Huang drama), Nvidia said SpaceX plans to adapt its Vera Rubin computing system for the first generation of satellites
SpaceX says the factory it’s building in Bastrop, Texas, could start turning out satellites for launch as early as late 2027.

claim: The first-generation AI1 satellite uses a space-optimized Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, could reach orbit by Q3 2027 according to Musk, and relies on Starship for heavy launches.

support.quote: Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.
SpaceX is counting on its Starship rocket to carry the heavy satellites into orbit in large numbers.

claim: The order waives Part 25 processing round and surety bond rules and sets a 15-year license term starting upon certification of the first operational satellite.

support.quote: SpaceX’s request for waiver of the Commission’s processing round rules in sections 25.156 and 25.157 is GRANTED.
SpaceX’s request for waiver of the Commission’s surety bond rules in section 25.165 is GRANTED.
The license term is 15 years and will begin at 3 a.m. EST on the date SpaceX certifies to the Commission that the first Starmind satellite has been successfully placed into orbit

claim: SpaceX must operate one satellite by November 25, 2033, 10% (100,000) by November 25, 2035, 50% (500,000) by November 25, 2038, and all 1,000,000 by November 25, 2040, with semiannual reports due January 1 and July 1.

support.quote: SpaceX must deploy one authorized space station, place it into its assigned orbit, and operate it in accordance with the station authorization no later than November 25, 2033.

SpaceX must deploy 10% of the maximum number of authorized space stations, place them in the assigned orbits, and operate them in accordance with the station authorization no later than November 25, 2035.

SpaceX must deploy 50% of the maximum number of authorized space stations, place them in the assigned orbits, and operate them in accordance with the station authorization no later than November 25, 2038.

SpaceX must launch the remaining space stations necessary to complete its authorized constellation, place them in their assigned orbits, and operate each in accordance with this authorization no later than November 25, 2040.
SpaceX must provide a semi-annual report, by January 1 and July 1 each year

claim: SpaceX withdrew its milestone-waiver request on October 19, 2026; missing any milestone voids the grant, and 100,000 satellites in 2035 is nearly nine times Starlink's active fleet.

support.quote: SpaceX originally requested waiver of the Commission’s milestone requirements altogether, but withdrew that request in favor of its request to apply the new milestones adopted in the Space Modernization R&O and FNPRM.
filed Oct. 19, 2026
SpaceX’s authorization will therefore become null and void if the authorized space stations are not deployed and operated as follows:
Two years later, the FCC expects 100,000 satellites to be operating. That's nearly nine times as many satellites as SpaceX's Starlink network has in orbit today.

claim: The Space Bureau approved atmospheric reentry disposal below 600 kilometers and deferred SpaceX's waiver request for the five-year reentry rule below 2,000 kilometers.

support.quote: SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions.

Because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements, SpaceX’s waiver request is deferred.

claim: SpaceX requested flexibility to dispose satellites above 600 km into Earth disposal or heliocentric orbits and must win approval of a modified debris plan before deploying above 600 km.

support.quote: flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.

Prior to deploying and operating any Starmind satellites that will not be disposed via atmospheric re-entry, SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules.

claim: Four of the six nominal bands sit above 600 kilometers, while in lower orbits SpaceX committed to initial testing below other operational systems and controlled, fully demisable ocean reentries.

support.quote: SpaceX’s orbital debris plan was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line.

These strategies include, for initial testing, deploying its satellites into orbits below other operational systems to ensure reentry, and for operational satellites, actively deorbiting in a controlled manner
and steering its satellites to reenter over the ocean. SpaceX commits that the design of each of its satellites is such that the satellite fully demises during reentry.
